question_text:
A 13-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of worsening fever, headache, photophobia, and nausea for 2 days. One week ago, she returned from summer camp. She has received all age-appropriate immunizations. Her temperature is 39.1°C (102.3°F). She is oriented to person, place, and time. Physical examination shows a maculopapular rash. There is rigidity of the neck; forced flexion of the neck results in involuntary flexion of the knees and hips. Cerebrospinal fluid studies show:
Opening pressure 120 mm H2O
Appearance Clear
Protein 47 mg/dL
Glucose 68 mg/dL
White cell count 280/mm3
Segmented neutrophils 15%
Lymphocytes 85%
Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?"?

### Enhanced Information Summary

The patient, a 13-year-old girl, presents with symptoms indicative of meningitis, including fever, headache, photophobia, nausea, neck rigidity, and a maculopapular rash. The cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis shows an elevated white cell count with a lymphocytic predominance (85% lymphocytes) and normal glucose levels, which are typical findings in viral meningitis rather than bacterial meningitis.

The reasoning chains and evidence paths suggest Echovirus as the most likely causative agent. This conclusion is supported by the fact that Echovirus is a common cause of viral meningitis in children and often presents with lymphocytic predominance in the CSF, as seen in this case. The normal glucose levels in the CSF also align more with viral infections, as bacterial infections typically present with decreased glucose levels.

The evidence paths related to cyclic AMP and its associations with symptoms like fever, photophobia, and neck stiffness do not directly contribute to identifying the causative organism but confirm the physiological responses associated with inflammation and meningitis.

The other pathogens listed as options (Listeria monocytogenes, Herpes simplex virus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis) are less likely given the CSF findings and the clinical presentation. Specifically, Neisseria meningitidis and Streptococcus pneumoniae typically show a predominance of neutrophils in the CSF and decreased glucose levels, which is not the case here. Herpes simplex virus more commonly causes encephalitis with a different clinical and CSF profile.

In conclusion, the clinical presentation, CSF findings, and the commonality of Echovirus in settings like summer camps where the patient had been recently, strongly suggest Echovirus as the causative agent of the meningitis in this patient.
